new_en: It is permitted to say to a shopkeeper, "Give me 4 eggs and 5 pomegranates," provided that he does not mention a price, a total measure, or a total count, such as saying, "You already owe me 50 nuts; give me another 50, so you will owe me 100." {Rama: Likewise, regarding a total price, the prohibition applies specifically when he says, "Give me merchandise for such and such an amount of money, so that you will owe me such and such an amount," but otherwise it is permitted. The same applies to a total measure: it is forbidden specifically in such a case, but otherwise it is permitted. Although it is generally forbidden to mention prices at all, that is regarding an item whose price is not fixed. Regarding an item whose price is known, if he merely tells the shopkeeper how much he needs, it is permitted, provided that he does not mention the total amount. [Or Zarua and Hagahot Ashiri, chapter Ein Tzedin] Although some are stringent regarding this matter, the custom has spread in these lands to be lenient in accordance with the view stated above.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: How documents are dated when Rosh Chodesh is 2 days. It contains 1 seif: When Rosh Chodesh is 2 days, on the first day one writes in documents, "on Rosh Chodesh," for it is the 30th day of the preceding month. The new month is counted from the second day, and on that day one writes, "on the first of the month." [Tur] {Rama: In a leap year, in the first Adar one writes simply "Adar," and in the second one writes "Adar Sheni." [Tur]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Shabbos HaGadol. It contains 1 seif: The Shabbos before Pesach is called Shabbos HaGadol because of the miracle that occurred on it. {Rama: The custom at Minchah is to recite the Haggadah from Avadim Hayinu through "to atone for all our sins," and Barchi Nafshi is omitted. [Minhagim]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The law of one who does not have guarded matzah. It contains 1 seif: One who has only a single kezayit of guarded matzah first recites the blessing over eating maror and eats it. When he finishes his meal, which he ate with matzah that was not guarded, he recites the blessing over eating matzah, eats that kezayit, and tastes nothing afterward. {Rama: One who has only 3 matzot for the 2 nights should, on the first night, recite HaMotzi and the blessing over eating matzah, and make the korech, all from the broken matzah, leaving the 2 whole matzot for the second night. [Abudarham in the name of Ibn Yarchi]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws observed during the days of the Omer. It contains 4 seifim: The custom is not to marry between Pesach and Shavuot until Lag BaOmer, because during that period the students of R' Akiva died. Erusin and kiddushin, however, are permitted, and if someone went ahead and married, he is not punished. {Rama: From Lag BaOmer onward everything is permitted. [Abudarham, Beit Yosef, and Minhagim]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of the days of supplication and the eve of Rosh Hashana. It contains 4 seifim: The custom is to rise during the night watch to recite Selichot and supplications from Rosh Chodesh Elul onward until Yom Kippur. {Rama: The custom of the people of Ashkenaz is not so. Rather, from Rosh Chodesh onward they begin to blow the shofar after Shacharit, and in some places they also blow it at Maariv. They rise during the night watch to recite Selichot on the Sunday before Rosh Hashana. If Rosh Hashana falls on Monday or Tuesday, they begin on the Sunday of the preceding week. [Minhagim] A mourner may not leave his house to enter the synagogue to hear Selichot, except on the eve of Rosh Hashana, when Selichot are greatly increased, in which case the mourner may enter the synagogue. [Piskei Mahari'a, siman 133] They should be meticulous to seek the most suitable prayer leader available, one who is greatest in Torah and good deeds, to lead Selichot and the Days of Awe; he should be 30 years old and also married. [Kol Bo] Nevertheless, all Jews are fit, provided that he is acceptable to the congregation. But if he forces himself upon them, they do not answer Amen after him. He must also intend in his prayer to discharge the obligation of every person. If he has an enemy and intends not to discharge that person's obligation, even his friends do not fulfill their obligation through his prayer. [Hagahot Minhagim Yeshanim] In some places the custom is that whoever leads Selichot also leads all the prayers of that day. [Kol Bo]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The repetition of Mussaf aloud and the order of the shofar blasts. It contains 4 seifim: The prayer leader repeats the Amidah, and they blow according to the order of the blessings: for Malchuyot, Tashrat once; for Zichronot, Tashat once; and for Shofarot, Tarat once. Nowadays the custom is to blow Tashrat 3 times for Malchuyot, Tashat 3 times for Zichronot, and Tarat 3 times for Shofarot. {Rama: Some say that Tashrat is blown once for Malchuyot, and likewise once for Zichronot and once for Shofarot. [Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Tam and Minhagim] This is the custom in these lands. The custom is to say after each set of blasts Hayom Harat Olam and Areshet. [Maharil] Even on Shabbos, when the shofar is not blown, Hayom Harat is recited, but Areshet is not. [Minhagim]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: On the remaining days, he recites the blessing over the sukkah before HaMotzi. The custom is to recite the blessing over the sukkah after HaMotzi, before tasting. {Rama: This is the practice on weekdays. On Shabbos and Yom Tov, when Kiddush is recited, he recites the blessing over the sukkah after Kiddush. [Mahariv] If he recited Kiddush in the house and eats in the sukkah, or vice versa, see above, siman 273, seif 2.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of the lulav. It contains 9 seifim: A lulav whose leaves have separated from one another but have not become loose and hanging like the leaves of a palm branch is valid, even if it was not bound. {Rama: Nevertheless, the preferred fulfillment of the mitzvah is with a lulav whose leaves are not completely separated. [Maggid Mishneh and Ran, chapter Lulav HaGazul]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Things that invalidate the 4 species. It contains 6 seifim: All 4 species are invalid if robbed or stolen, whether before the owner has despaired of recovering them or after he has despaired. But if one robbed an item and acquired it through an act unrelated to performance of the mitzvah, such as one who robbed a lulav and trimmed it, it is valid, because he acquired it through a physical change. Nevertheless, he should not recite a blessing over it. Some say that a robbed or stolen item is invalid only for the thief or robber himself, but for others it is valid on the remaining days other than the first day. {Rama: For this reason, one should be careful that a Jew not personally cut one of the 4 species for his lulav, because land cannot be acquired through robbery, and ordinarily non-Jews are presumed to have robbed land, so the item may come into his hand through robbery. Rather, the non-Jew should cut it and the Jew should purchase it from him. [Responsa Rashba, siman 852; Hagahot Ashiri, end of chapter Lulav HaGazul] There is no distinction in this respect between Eretz Yisrael and outside Eretz Yisrael. [Or Zarua] A lulav that a non-Jew bound and prepared is valid, just as a sukkah made by a non-Jew is valid. [Mordechai, Hilchot Ketanot]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The sukkah and its decorations are forbidden throughout Shemini Atzeret as well. It contains 1 seif: The sukkah and its decorations are forbidden on Shemini Atzeret. Outside Eretz Yisrael, where 2 days of Yom Tov are observed, they are also forbidden on the ninth day, because it may be the eighth. If Shabbos begins immediately after the final Yom Tov of the festival, the custom is not to make use of the sukkah decorations until after Shabbos; some permit it. {Rama: Some have the custom, when leaving the sukkah, to say, "May it be Your will that we merit to sit in the sukkah of Leviathan." [Kol Bo] It is forbidden to prepare on Yom Tov for the following night of Yom Tov. Therefore it is forbidden to set up the tables and benches in the house for the night, because this constitutes preparation. [Hagahot Maimoniyot and Maharil]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Tachanun is not recited on the 14th and 15th of the first Adar, and the law of fasting and eulogizing on those days. It contains 1 seif: On the 14th and 15th of the first Adar one does not fall on his face in Tachanun and does not recite the psalm "May Hashem answer you on the day of distress." Eulogizing and fasting are forbidden, but the other Purim practices are not observed. Some say that even eulogizing and fasting are permitted. {Rama: The custom follows the first view. Some say that one is obligated to increase feasting and rejoicing on the 14th of the first Adar. [Tur in the name of Rif] This is not the custom. Nevertheless, one should add somewhat to the meal in order to satisfy the stringent opinions. [Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of Semak] "A cheerful heart has a continual feast."}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of prayer and its time. It contains 8 seifim: The proper time for Shacharit is to begin with sunrise, as it is written, "They shall fear You with the sun." If one prayed from dawn, after the eastern horizon became illuminated, he has fulfilled his obligation. Its time extends until the end of 4 seasonal hours, which is one-third of the day. If one erred or transgressed and prayed after 4 hours but before midday, although he does not receive the reward for prayer in its proper time, he nevertheless receives the reward for prayer. {Rama: After midday it is forbidden to pray Shacharit. [Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba, chapter Tefillat HaShachar] See above at the beginning of siman 108.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: One must have intention in his prayer. It contains 5 seifim: One who prays must concentrate in his heart on the meaning of the words he utters with his lips, and should think as though the Divine Presence stands before him. He should remove all distracting thoughts until his thought and intention in prayer are pure. He should consider that if he were speaking before a flesh-and-blood king, he would arrange his words and concentrate on them carefully so as not to stumble; all the more so before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed is He, who examines all thoughts. This is how the pious and men of deeds would conduct themselves: they would seclude themselves and concentrate on their prayer until they reached a state of detachment from corporeality and strengthening of the intellectual faculty, approaching the level of prophecy. If another thought comes to him during prayer, he should remain silent until the thought passes. He should think of matters that humble the heart and direct it toward his Father in Heaven, and should not think of matters involving frivolity. {Rama: Before prayer he should contemplate the exaltedness of God and the lowliness of man, and remove all human pleasures from his heart. [Rabbeinu Yonah, beginning of chapter Ein Omdin] A person may not kiss his young children in the synagogue, in order to establish in his heart that there is no love like the love of the Omnipresent, blessed is He. [Binyamin Ze'ev, siman 163; Agudah, chapter Keitzad Mevarchin]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: It is forbidden to have marital relations during years of famine, except for one who is childless, meaning one who has no children. {Rama: See also siman 574, seif 4. The same applies to other calamities comparable to famine. [Yerushalmi, Taanis]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If non-Jews built a house for a Jew on Shabbos in a prohibited manner, it is proper to be stringent and not enter it. {Rama: If, however, the Jew stipulated with the non-Jew that he not perform melacha for him on Shabbos, and the non-Jew nevertheless performed it against the Jew's wishes in order to complete his work sooner, there is no concern. [Mordechai, beginning of chapter Mi SheHafach; Rabbeinu Yeruham; Beit Yosef; see also siman 543]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: A Jew and a non-Jew who jointly own a field, oven, bathhouse, water mill, or merchandise in a shop: if, when they first entered the partnership, they stipulated that the profits of Shabbos, whether little or much, would belong solely to the non-Jew, and that the profits of 1 weekday corresponding to Shabbos would belong solely to the Jew, it is permitted. If they did not stipulate this at the outset, then when they later divide the profits, the non-Jew takes all the profits of the Shabbosos and the Jew takes the corresponding profits of the weekdays; the remainder is divided equally. If the profits of Shabbos are not known separately, they may divide all the profits equally. {Rama: Some authorities say that all of this applies only when each partner's work is fixed for a particular day, but if they work together whenever they wish and the non-Jew works on Shabbos of his own accord, they may divide all the profits equally, because the Jew did not instruct the non-Jew to work for him and the melacha is not recognizable as belonging to the Jew. [Rosh and other authorities]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Where they did not stipulate at the outset, there is a remedy: the seller may return to them the purchase money for the property, or they may sell it to another person and then repurchase it jointly while making the stipulation at the time of purchase. If they entered a partnership in a shop without stipulating, each should take back his share and they should dissolve the partnership, after which they may enter a new partnership and stipulate from the outset. If they accepted land to work jointly, they should dissolve the partnership and waive their claims against one another, and afterward enter a new partnership and stipulate from the outset. {Rama: If the Jew wishes to lease his share to the non-Jew for Shabbos, or hire the non-Jew as a contractor, it is permitted, as explained above at the end of siman 244 regarding customs duties and minting, where it is permitted, and all the more so here.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The law of non-Jews who carry letters on Shabbos. It contains 6 seifim: A person may send a letter with a non-Jew even close to nightfall on Friday, provided that he fixes a price with him and does not tell him to travel on Shabbos. If no price was fixed, then if there is a fixed postal station in the city, the Jew may send it even on Friday, provided that enough time remains in the day for the non-Jew to reach a house near the city wall before Shabbos. If there is no fixed postal station, one may not send it on Friday unless there is enough time for it to reach the house to which it is addressed before Shabbos. {Rama: Some permit sending it even where no price was fixed and there is no fixed postal station in the city, provided that it is sent on Thursday or earlier. In a case of need, one may rely upon this view.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If the non-Jew carries the letter without payment, it is permitted even if it was given to him on Friday, because the non-Jew does this of his own accord merely to show gratitude to the Jew for a benefit he previously received from him, and it is therefore regarded as though a price had been fixed. {Rama: Some disagree and hold that whenever the non-Jew does it without payment it is forbidden, and it is proper to be stringent. But where the non-Jew initiates the matter and tells the Jew that he will go for him without payment, his intent is certainly for the benefit he previously received from the Jew, and it is permitted. [Beit Yosef]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: One who has a non-Jewish employee hired for a year or longer may not send a letter with him on Friday. {Rama: If, however, he hired him only for the task of carrying letters, some permit it, as explained above in siman 244, seif 5.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Preparing the Shabbos meal. It contains 2 seifim: One should rise early on Friday morning to prepare the needs of Shabbos. Even if he has several servants to serve him, he should endeavor to prepare something himself in honor of Shabbos, as Rav Chisda would cut vegetables finely, Rabbah and Rav Yosef would chop wood, R' Zeira would kindle the fire, and Rav Nachman would clean the house and exchange the weekday utensils for Shabbos utensils. From them every person should learn, and should not say, "It is beneath my dignity," because this is the honor of Shabbos. {Rama: One should also sharpen his knife on Friday so that it will be ready for eating, for this too is an honor of Shabbos and prepares him for eating. [Kol Bo; Beit Yosef in the name of Sefer Chayei Olam]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: It is permitted to give one's garments to a non-Jewish launderer and hides to a tanner close to nightfall on Friday, if he fixed a price with him or the non-Jew does the work as a favor, provided that he does not tell him to do it on Shabbos and the non-Jew performs the work in his own premises. If the Jew sees him performing the work on Shabbos, then where he is doing it as a favor the Jew must tell him not to perform it on Shabbos. {Rama: If no price was fixed, it is forbidden to give it to him on Friday. See siman 247 regarding the distinction when the non-Jew works without payment as a favor. Even if he gave it to him several days before Shabbos, where the circumstances make it appear that the non-Jew is acting on the Jew's behalf on Shabbos, the restrictions explained there apply.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of a kirah and an oven, regarding placing a pot upon them before Shabbos. It contains 5 seifim: A kirah is made like a large pot, with room on its opening above for 2 pots. If it was heated with olive refuse or with wood, it is forbidden before Shabbos to place a cooked dish upon it to remain there, unless the dish is fully cooked and further reduction is detrimental to it, so that there is no concern that one may stir the coals, or unless the food is completely raw and has not cooked at all, because when it is raw one puts it out of mind until the next day and it can cook throughout the night without stirring the coals. But if it has cooked somewhat and is not fully cooked, or even if it is fully cooked but further reduction improves it, we are concerned that one may stir the coals, and it is forbidden to leave it there unless the kirah was garuf, meaning that all the coals were removed, or katum, meaning that the coals were covered with ashes to reduce their heat. If he placed a raw piece into the pot, it is permitted as though the entire dish were raw, because by doing so he puts it out of mind. Even when the kirah is neither garuf nor katum, it is permitted to place a pot adjacent to it on the outside. If it was heated with straw or stubble, one may leave a pot upon it even if it is neither garuf nor katum. {Rama: If 2 kirahs adjoin one another with an earthenware wall between them, one being garuf and katum and the other not garuf and katum, it is permitted to leave food on the garuf and katum one even though it receives additional heat from the one that is not garuf and katum. [Gemara, chapter Kirah]} An oven, even if heated with straw or stubble, is forbidden even for placing a pot adjacent to it, even if it is garuf and katum. {Rama: All this applies while it remains hot enough that the hand recoils from it. [Hagahot Mordechai]} All the more so is it forbidden to leave a pot inside it or on top of it. A kupach, which has room for 1 pot, has the law of a kirah if heated with straw or stubble, and the law of an oven if heated with olive refuse or wood. Our ovens have the law of a kirah. [Ran, beginning of chapter Kirah; Kol Bo; and so is implied by Rashi.] If one forgot and left a dish there, if it was fully cooked it is permitted even if further reduction improves it. If it had begun cooking but was not fully cooked, it is forbidden until after Shabbos. If he deliberately left it there in violation of the law, it is forbidden in both cases. {Rama: It remains forbidden after Shabbos for the amount of time required for the act to have been done. [Hagahot Ashiri; Rambam, chapter 3] If a non-Jew returned the pots on Shabbos, the law is like one who forgot and left them there. [Hagahot Ashiri] If a Jew returned them, the law is like one who deliberately left them there. [Hagahot Mordechai] If further reduction is detrimental to the food, it is permitted, because he derived no benefit from the prohibition. [Beit Yosef; see above at the beginning of siman 227]} Some say that whenever the food has cooked to the degree of ma'achal ben Derusai, meaning the degree at which Ben Derusai would eat food that was not fully cooked, or it is fully cooked and further reduction improves it, it may be left on a kirah. {Rama: Or even on top of an oven. [Maggid Mishneh, chapter 3; Hagahot Mordechai; Maimoniyot, chapter 3; beginning of chapter Kirah; Beit Yosef]} This applies even if it was heated with olive refuse or wood and even if it is neither garuf nor katum. The requirements of garuf and katum, and of heating with straw or stubble, were stated only where the food had begun to cook but had not reached ma'achal ben Derusai. The same restrictions apply if one removed the pot and wishes to return it on Shabbos. If one forgot and left a dish that had begun cooking but had not reached ma'achal ben Derusai, it is forbidden, and all the more so if he deliberately left it there. {Rama: The custom is to be lenient in accordance with the latter view.} All of this, regarding leaving a pot, applies when the pot sits on an iron stand or on stones and does not touch the coals. But insulating a pot directly upon coals is forbidden according to all opinions. {Rama: Some say that even if the pot stands directly upon the fire, as long as it is uncovered on top it is not considered insulation and is permitted, and this is the custom. They are careful, however, to detach it somewhat from the fire before Shabbos so that a Jew will be able to remove it. If it was not detached from the fire and he finds it upon the fire on Shabbos, it should be removed by a non-Jew. If no non-Jew is available, a Jew may remove it, but he must take it gently and avoid moving the coals. If he nevertheless moves them slightly unintentionally, it is permitted because this is an unintended act. [Mordechai, beginning of chapter Kirah; Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 7]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; all 6 Rama glosses restored in source order.
